title: Releasing a game on Steam with partial AI-generated graphics
author: titinho15

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body:
"Can they detect?"
Maybe, maybe not.

The point is that you're lying if you tell them there's no AI involved, so if they detect, they'll be pissed.

replies.author: titinho15
replies.body: Fair point, but if I tell them, I cannot release my game which is definitely not the way of ending potentially a year of work :\\ I very well knew AI-generated stuff are gray area when I started working on the game, still, I had so much excitement and motivation to finally be able to create my dream game with the small funds I had even though I'm a programmer, with little to no skills in graphics.

comments.author: Roshakim
comments.body:
I don't know for sure if steam has an anti-ai automated check system. They might. If they do, it's only as good as it was trained. Meaning, I imagine it could only detect whatever models it was trained on, likely only the most popular ones.

If I was tasked with making an anti-AI detect system for steam, I'd create multiple models, each of which was trained on the most popular models out there. I'd also create different models which are cross model and look for common inconsistencies like multiple or missing fingers, legs, toes, and situations where clothing warps into the background or hair. Also eyes are usually fucked up, so I'd look for that as well.

Then anything triggered, I'd send for manual review as part of a QA check to avoid false positives.

If they have such a system, it's probably like the above. If they don't, then it's probably just human review. The most common models have similar issues / appearance and are easy to spot by someone familiar.

Less common models, and more specialized / advanced models are much more difficult as they keep getting better and better. Lots of styles out there and very difficult to keep up, and you massively increase the risk of false positives.

When it comes to non-character AI, it gets more difficult, but doable. The more complex the image, the easier a model can be trained to detect AI gen.

AI gen for simple textures is much more difficult if not an almost impossible problem to solve except for situations where there are a few very dominant models that folks use. Then you can train to catch those. But beyond that, it's probably a lost cause and false positive land.

So lessons learned? If you want to use AI and get past any anti-AI system, then you need to make sure you are using a model / stylization / features which are not common AND you avoid common signs of AI gen. The simpler the images you gen, the less likely you will have trouble.

If you are generating 2d full character images including backgrounds, like for an anime visual novel - these are the things that are MUCH MORE LIKELY to get caught either by anti-AI tech or human manual review. The simpler, and more specialized -> far, far less likely if not practically impossible to detect / or for steam to be sure it isn't a false positive.

My 2 cents.

replies.author: titinho15
replies.body: Thanks for your input! My game has a digital painting/speed painting style which makes it very easy to adjust/change generated images so my characters don't have those common AI-generated problems. I also repaint most of them and create separate layers to animate them, they look very much handmade. Though there are some icons that I did not touch in PS, I feel like they are so small there is no way they can identify those as AI-generated. The backgrounds are the ones that I'm afraid of since even though they 100% fit the rest of the game style they still look AI-generated a little bit, no matter how much I tweak them. I might hire a graphic artist to do the backgrounds and store assets just to be sure.

replies.author: Roshakim
replies.body:
If you are using any popular models / styles I'd worry, esp on more complicated gens like the backgrounds. 

I saw you are using MidJourney. I haven't used it and am not familiar with it. I thought MJ had a commercial friendly license? I thought Steam's big concern was proving copyright ownership? If MJ has a commercial friendly license, that should cover it? Double check on this if so.

I use Stable Diffusion which has easily hundreds of different base models, and then you can combine models, and then stack LORAs / embeddings on top and other things which can dramatically change the style into something very specific and unique and makes it look nothing like other generic AI gen stuff out there all over the place. So going down that rabbit hole would pay off I would think. Time heavy investment upfront to find your style and figure things out though.
